## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module               Deep Learning and Signal Processing: Introduction and Industrial Applications
  Official title       Apprentissage profond et traitement du signal, introduction et applications industrielles
  Instructors          T. COURTAT (master-mva.com, 2026–2027)
  Period               Semester 1 · period 1 (28/09/2026 – 08/01/2027)
  Credits and volume   5 ECTS · 30 h (lectures 12 h, labs 18 h) per the Université Paris-Saclay programme table
  Label                [Modelling]{.badge .label}[Track I&I]{.badge .track}
  Language             French (“Le cours sera donné en français”, master-mva.com); no distance learning (Université Paris-Saclay)
  Assessment           “Evaluation Continue non Intégrale” (Université Paris-Saclay): continuous assessment, non-integral regime; components and weights not displayed
  Prerequisites        Data structures, Python programming, L3-level linear algebra, differential calculus, probability and statistics, basics of machine learning (master-mva.com; the Université Paris-Saclay page lists the same items except the last)
  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: a student with an M1 in mathematics, computer science or physics who has trained a classifier before and wants to know when a neural network beats — or loses to — decades of signal-processing know-how on radio, radar, speech and vibration data.

**Empirical first**: on 256 samples of a narrowband transmitter at −15 dB, the textbook energy detector reaches an AUC of only 0.64, while a periodogram peak search and a logistic regression on sorted spectra both reach 0.82 (Code 5.7). A bearing whose raw vibration looks Gaussian (kurtosis 3.3) shows, once band-passed and demodulated, a line 28 times the background at the fault frequency of 90 Hz (Code 9.3). The course explains both numbers.

The course asks what deep learning brings to signal processing, one industrial use case at a time: spectrum sensing for cognitive radio, radar emitter identification, speaker recognition, restoration of damaged audio and predictive maintenance. Each case starts from the physics, builds the classical chain, then revisits it with learning. It shares its Fourier and statistical tools with [Machine Learning for Time Series](../s1-time-series/index.html) and [Deep Learning](../s1-deep-learning/index.html), and prepares [Audio Signal Processing: Time–Frequency Analysis](../s2-audio-time-frequency/index.html) and [Detection Theory and Industrial Applications](../s2-detection-theory/index.html).

### What you will be able to do

-   Model a sensor signal in complex baseband, sample it without aliasing and choose DFT and STFT parameters from a resolution budget.
-   Design and analyse linear filters, including the matched filter and radar pulse compression.
-   Compute and interpret spectrograms, scalograms, mel spectra and MFCCs, and explain the time–frequency trade-off behind them.
-   Formulate detection as a Neyman–Pearson test, size an energy detector and compute its SNR wall.
-   Train, evaluate and compare classical classifiers and clustering algorithms on signal features, with leakage-free splits.
-   Build and train 1D and 2D convolutional, recurrent and attention-based networks on raw signals and spectrograms in PyTorch.
-   Deinterleave radar pulse trains with clustering and TOA-difference histograms, and explain RF fingerprinting.
-   Build a speaker-recognition chain from GMM-UBM to deep embeddings, and enrol new classes with few-shot prototypes.
-   Restore degraded audio with Wiener gains, autoregressive interpolation and learned masks.
-   Detect bearing faults with envelope analysis, condition indicators and anomaly detection with a controlled false-alarm rate.
-   Prove a depth-separation result and argue, case by case, when a classical pipeline should be preferred to a deep one.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026–2027)

The course description on master-mva.com, repeated on the Université Paris-Saclay page, sets the objective of understanding what deep-learning approaches can bring to signal-processing problems through several industrial use cases, for instance radar emitter identification, signal detection for cognitive radio, speaker recognition, the reconstruction of altered audio signals and predictive maintenance.

For each use case, the description announces that “classical” processing chains are studied, discussed and implemented in labs, then revisited with a “learning” approach. Each case begins with its operational context and a model of the physics of the problem, so that students acquire a culture of the application domains.

The theory part introduces signal-processing tools (time–frequency and time–scale representations, filtering) and machine-learning tools (supervised and unsupervised approaches, the main families of classification and clustering algorithms, optimisation, gradient descent, the basics of deep learning and the main network architectures).

Through these back-and-forths between theory and practice, the course tries to answer the question “what makes the depth of deep learning?”. The master-mva.com page adds that this industry-oriented course is also an occasion to discuss how research is organised in companies. The organisation is 12 h of lectures and 18 h of labs, taught in French; the Université Paris-Saclay page presents the course as module 1 of the “Industrie et Ingénierie” (I&I) track.

### Where this course fits in the programme

Official prerequisites: data structures, Python programming, linear algebra, differential calculus, probability and statistics at L3 level, and the basics of machine learning (the last item appears on master-mva.com only).

-   **Preparation** — the refreshers [Probability and Statistics](../s0-refresher-probability-statistics/index.html), [Linear Algebra, Analysis and Optimization](../s0-refresher-linear-algebra-optimization/index.html) and [Scientific Python, NumPy and PyTorch](../s0-refresher-python-scientific-computing/index.html). The catalogue's calendar marks the refresher courses as mandatory for the I&I track.
-   **Related courses of semester 1** — [Machine Learning for Time Series](../s1-time-series/index.html), [Deep Learning](../s1-deep-learning/index.html), [Introduction to Statistical Learning](../s1-intro-statistical-learning/index.html), [Convex Optimization and Applications in Machine Learning](../s1-convex-optimization/index.html) and [Theoretical Foundations of Deep Learning](../s1-theoretical-foundations-dl/index.html); within the I&I track, [The Machine Intelligence of Images](../s1-machine-intelligence-images/index.html) and [Statistical Learning for Scientific Imaging and Physical Measurements: Geosciences](../s1-ml-geosciences/index.html).
-   **Courses that build on it (semester 2)** — [Audio Signal Processing: Time–Frequency Analysis](../s2-audio-time-frequency/index.html), [Audio Signal Analysis, Indexing and Transformations](../s2-audio-analysis-indexing/index.html), [Algorithms for Speech and Natural Language Processing](../s2-speech-nlp/index.html), [Detection Theory and Industrial Applications](../s2-detection-theory/index.html) and [Remote Sensing Data](../s2-remote-sensing/index.html).

### Course outline

-   **Review: Fourier bases, Gaussian noise and the chain rule** — the M1 tools used everywhere else, with the chi-square law of noise energy.
-   **Signals, sampling and filtering** — complex baseband, the sampling theorem, the DFT, LTI filters and the matched filter.
-   **Time–frequency and time–scale representations** — STFT and spectrogram, the uncertainty principle, wavelets, filter banks, mel spectrum and MFCC.
-   **The machine-learning toolbox** — supervised and unsupervised learning, classifier families, clustering, metrics and gradient descent.
-   **Deep learning: basics and main architectures** — backpropagation, CNN, RNN, autoencoders, attention, training practice and a first answer on depth.
-   **Signal detection for cognitive radio** — Neyman–Pearson, the energy detector and its SNR wall, cyclostationary and learned detectors.
-   **Radar emitter identification** — pulse descriptor words, deinterleaving, clustering and emitter fingerprinting.
-   **Speaker recognition and few-shot learning** — the source–filter model, GMM-UBM, x-vectors, prototypes for new speakers.
-   **Reconstruction of altered audio signals** — Wiener gains, autoregressive gap interpolation, sparse inpainting and learned masks.
-   **Predictive maintenance** — bearing physics, envelope analysis, condition indicators, anomaly detection and remaining useful life.
-   **Synthesis: what makes deep learning deep, and research in industry** — depth, invariance and stability, hybrid models, the industrial research cycle.
-   **Research directions and open problems** — self-supervised signal models, open-set recognition, domain shift and model-based learning (self-study).

### How to study this module

-   Read [ch. 0](#ch0) before the first session if Fourier series or Gaussian vectors are rusty; the three refreshers cover the rest.
-   Chapters 5 to 9 share one structure: operational context and physics, classical chain, learned chain, comparison. Run the classical code before the learned one, and write down what each assumes.
-   Keep a lab notebook with one table per use case: data, classical result, learned result, cost, and what failed. It feeds the projects and [ch. 10](#ch10).
-   Do the exercises listed in the session plan after each session; the ★ ones check the computations, the ★★ ones the proofs.
-   All code runs on a laptop CPU in seconds with NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn and PyTorch, on synthetic data; no download is needed.

## 0. Review: Fourier bases, Gaussian noise and the chain rule {#ch0}

Every later chapter projects signals on Fourier-type bases, models noise as Gaussian and differentiates compositions of functions. This review fixes the notation and proves the three facts used most often: the discrete Fourier basis is orthonormal, Gaussian vectors stay Gaussian under linear maps, and the energy of Gaussian noise follows a chi-square law.

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — Inner product, orthonormal basis]{.tag} On $\mathbb{C}^N$ the inner product and the norm are
$$
\langle x, y \rangle = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n]\, \overline{y[n]}, \qquad \|x\|^2 = \langle x, x \rangle .
$$

A family $(e_k)$ is an orthonormal basis when $\langle e_k, e_l \rangle = \delta_{kl}$ and it spans $\mathbb{C}^N$. Every signal then expands on it, and its energy is the sum of the squared coefficients (Parseval):
$$
x = \sum_k \langle x, e_k \rangle\, e_k, \qquad \|x\|^2 = \sum_k |\langle x, e_k \rangle|^2 .
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.2 — The discrete Fourier basis]{.tag} The vectors
$$
e_k[n] = \frac{1}{\sqrt N}\, e^{2i\pi k n / N}, \qquad k = 0, \dots, N-1,
$$
form an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{C}^N$.

::: proof
For $k \neq l$, put $q = e^{2i\pi (k - l)/N}$. Then $q \neq 1$ and $q^N = 1$, so the geometric sum vanishes:
$$
\langle e_k, e_l \rangle = \frac1N \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} q^n = \frac1N\, \frac{1 - q^N}{1 - q} = 0 .
$$

For $k = l$, every term equals $1/N$ and the sum is $1$. Finally, $N$ orthonormal vectors are linearly independent, hence a basis of a space of dimension $N$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

The numbers $\sqrt N \langle x, e_k \rangle$ are the DFT of ch. 1.3, and Parseval says that the DFT preserves energy up to the factor $N$.
::::

::: def
[Definition 0.3 — Gaussian vectors and complex white noise]{.tag} A random vector $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is Gaussian, written $x \sim \mathcal N(\mu, \Sigma)$, when every linear form $a^\top x$ is a real Gaussian variable. For an invertible covariance $\Sigma$ its density is
$$
p(x) = (2\pi)^{-d/2} \det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\Big(-\frac12 (x - \mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (x - \mu)\Big).
$$

A complex variable $w = u + iv$ is circular Gaussian, $w \sim \mathcal{CN}(0, \sigma^2)$, when $u$ and $v$ are independent with law $\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2/2)$; then $\mathbb E|w|^2 = \sigma^2$.

In this course, **white Gaussian noise** of power $\sigma^2$ is a sequence of independent $\mathcal{CN}(0, \sigma^2)$ samples (or $\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)$ for real signals). Its expected power is the same at every frequency.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.4 — Linear maps and the energy of Gaussian noise]{.tag}

1.  If $x \sim \mathcal N(\mu, \Sigma)$, $A \in \mathbb R^{m \times d}$ and $b \in \mathbb R^m$, then
    $$
    Ax + b \sim \mathcal N(A\mu + b,\ A \Sigma A^\top).
    $$
2.  If $z_1, \dots, z_k$ are independent $\mathcal N(0, 1)$, then $\sum_i z_i^2$ follows the chi-square law $\chi^2_k$, with mean $k$ and variance $2k$.
3.  For $N$ samples of complex white noise of power $\sigma^2$:
    $$
    \frac{2}{\sigma^2} \sum_{n=1}^{N} |w[n]|^2 \sim \chi^2_{2N}.
    $$

::: proof
1.  A linear form of $Ax + b$ is $(A^\top a)^\top x + a^\top b$: a linear form of $x$ plus a constant, hence Gaussian. The mean and the covariance follow from the linearity of expectation.
2.  The mean is $k\, \mathbb E z^2 = k$. Since $\mathbb E z^4 = 3$, each term has variance $3 - 1 = 2$, and independence adds the variances.
3.  Write $|w[n]|^2 = u^2 + v^2$ with $u, v$ independent $\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2/2)$. Then $2|w[n]|^2 / \sigma^2$ is a sum of two squared standard Gaussians, and the $N$ independent samples give $2N$ squares. [∎]{.qed}
:::

The chi-square law sets the threshold of the energy detector (ch. 5.3) and of the Mahalanobis alarm (ch. 9.4).
::::

::: def
[Definition 0.5 — Jacobian, gradient and the chain rule]{.tag} For a differentiable $f : \mathbb R^d \to \mathbb R^m$, the Jacobian $J_f(x) \in \mathbb R^{m \times d}$ collects the partial derivatives $\partial f_i / \partial x_j$. For $m = 1$ the gradient is $\nabla f = J_f^\top$. For a composition $h = g \circ f$,
$$
J_h(x) = J_g(f(x))\, J_f(x).
$$

Two gradients are used repeatedly. For a symmetric matrix $A$:
$$
\nabla_x \Big(\frac12 x^\top A x - b^\top x\Big) = Ax - b, \qquad \nabla_x\, \frac12 \|y - Hx\|^2 = H^\top (Hx - y).
$$
:::

::: ex
[Example 0.6 — Power ratios in decibels]{.tag} Signal-processing results are quoted in decibels: a power ratio $r$ is $10 \log_{10} r$ dB.

-   A signal of power $0.1$ in noise of power $1$ has an SNR of $-10$ dB; at $-20$ dB the ratio is $0.01$.
-   Halving an amplitude divides the power by $4$, that is $-6.02$ dB.
-   Coherently integrating $N$ samples of a known signal multiplies the SNR by $N$ (ch. 1.6); with $N = 1000$:
$$
\text{gain} = 10 \log_{10} 1000 = 30 \text{ dB}.
$$
:::

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 0
:::

-   The discrete Fourier vectors form an orthonormal basis; energy is preserved (Parseval).
-   Gaussian vectors stay Gaussian under affine maps; the energy of white Gaussian noise is a scaled chi-square variable.
-   Gradients of compositions are products of Jacobians — the whole of backpropagation (ch. 4.2).
-   Decibels turn power ratios into sums; integration over $N$ samples buys $10 \log_{10} N$ dB.
::::

## 1. Signals, sampling and filtering {#ch1}

A sensor delivers a continuous waveform; a computer stores a finite list of numbers. This chapter states when the list loses nothing (sampling), how to read its frequency content (DFT), and how to transform it linearly (filters), up to the matched filter that every radar and receiver uses.

### 1.1 Signals and complex baseband

Radio, radar and many vibration signals are narrowband: their energy sits in a band of width $B$ around a carrier $f_c$ with $B \ll f_c$. Sampling them directly would require more than $2 f_c$ samples per second; one samples instead the slowly varying envelope.

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Complex baseband (complex envelope)]{.tag} A real bandpass signal of carrier $f_c$ is written
$$
x(t) = \mathrm{Re}\big\{ s(t)\, e^{2i\pi f_c t} \big\}, \qquad s(t) = I(t) + i\, Q(t),
$$
where the complex envelope $s$ has its spectrum in $[-B/2, B/2]$.

The receiver mixes $x$ with a cosine and a sine at the carrier and low-pass filters the products. This yields the in-phase and quadrature components $I$ and $Q$: the **IQ samples**.
:::

::: ex
[Example 1.2 — Why IQ samples]{.tag} An X-band radar signal at $f_c = 10$ GHz with $B = 20$ MHz would need more than $2(f_c + B/2) \approx 20.02$ GHz if sampled as a real signal. Its complex envelope, of bandwidth $20$ MHz, needs only $20$ million complex samples per second.

$$
\text{rate reduction} \approx \frac{20\,020 \text{ MHz}}{2 \times 20 \text{ MHz}} \approx 500 .
$$

Every radio and radar data set of chapters 5 and 6 is a sequence of IQ samples.
:::

### 1.2 Sampling and aliasing

The Fourier transform of a finite-energy signal is $X(f) = \int x(t)\, e^{-2i\pi f t}\, dt$. A sampling period $T_s$ defines the rate $f_s = 1/T_s$ and the samples $x[n] = x(n T_s)$.

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.3 — Sampling theorem (Shannon–Nyquist)]{.tag} Let $x$ be integrable and square-integrable, with $X(f) = 0$ for $|f| \geq f_s/2$. Then $x$ is determined by its samples, through the interpolation formula
$$
x(t) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb Z} x(nT_s)\, \mathrm{sinc}\Big(\frac{t - nT_s}{T_s}\Big), \qquad \mathrm{sinc}(u) = \frac{\sin \pi u}{\pi u}.
$$

::: proof
*Sketch.* The Poisson summation formula gives the spectrum of the sampled sequence as the periodisation of $X$:
$$
\sum_{n} x(nT_s)\, e^{-2i\pi f n T_s} = f_s \sum_{k \in \mathbb Z} X(f - k f_s).
$$

When $X$ vanishes outside $(-f_s/2, f_s/2)$, the copies do not overlap. Multiplying by the ideal low-pass window, equal to $1/f_s$ on $[-f_s/2, f_s/2]$ and $0$ elsewhere, therefore returns exactly $X$.

In time, multiplication by this window is convolution with its inverse transform, the sinc kernel scaled by $T_s$, which is the interpolation formula. [∎]{.qed}
:::

When the hypothesis fails, the copies overlap: a component at frequency $f$ reappears at $f - k f_s$ for the integer $k$ that brings it into $[-f_s/2, f_s/2]$. This is **aliasing**, and no processing after sampling can undo it; an analogue anti-aliasing filter must act before the converter.
::::

### 1.3 The discrete Fourier transform

::: def
[Definition 1.4 — DFT and frequency resolution]{.tag} The DFT of $x \in \mathbb C^N$ and its inverse are
$$
X[k] = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n]\, e^{-2i\pi k n / N}, \qquad x[n] = \frac1N \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} X[k]\, e^{2i\pi k n / N}.
$$

Bin $k$ corresponds to the frequency $k f_s / N$ (bins above $N/2$ to negative frequencies), so the bin spacing is $f_s / N$: resolution is bought with observation time $N / f_s$. The fast Fourier transform (Cooley and Tukey, 1965) computes the DFT in $\mathcal O(N \log N)$ operations.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.5 — Circular convolution theorem]{.tag} Define the circular convolution
$$
(x \circledast h)[n] = \sum_{m=0}^{N-1} x[m]\, h[(n - m) \bmod N].
$$
Then its DFT is the product of the DFTs:
$$
\mathrm{DFT}(x \circledast h)[k] = X[k]\, H[k].
$$

::: proof
Substitute and exchange the sums, with $\omega = e^{-2i\pi/N}$:
$$
\sum_n \sum_m x[m]\, h[(n - m) \bmod N]\, \omega^{kn} = \sum_m x[m]\, \omega^{km} \sum_n h[(n - m) \bmod N]\, \omega^{k(n - m)}.
$$

Since $\omega^{kN} = 1$, the inner sum runs over a full period of $h$ whatever $m$ is, and equals $H[k]$. The outer sum is $X[k]$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

Linear (non-circular) convolution is obtained by zero-padding both signals to length at least $N_x + N_h - 1$: this is how long filters are applied by FFT.
::::

A tone whose frequency falls between two bins spreads its energy over all bins: this is **spectral leakage**, caused by the implicit rectangular window of the finite observation. Tapering windows trade a wider main lobe for lower side lobes. The highest side lobe sits at about $-13$ dB for the rectangular window, $-31$ dB for Hann and $-43$ dB for Hamming.

The code below shows aliasing — a 7 kHz tone sampled at 10 kHz appears at 3 kHz — and designs a low-pass filter with a Hamming window (ch. 1.5).

```python
# Code 1.6 — aliasing, and a windowed-sinc low-pass filter
import numpy as np
from scipy import signal

fs = 10_000                          # sampling rate (Hz)
t = np.arange(0, 0.1, 1 / fs)        # 1000 samples
x = np.sin(2 * np.pi * 7_000 * t)    # a 7 kHz tone, above fs / 2
X = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x))
f = np.fft.rfftfreq(len(x), 1 / fs)
print("apparent frequency:", f[np.argmax(X)], "Hz")

# 101-tap windowed-sinc low-pass filter, cut-off 1 kHz
h = signal.firwin(101, 1_000, fs=fs, window="hamming")
_, H = signal.freqz(h, worN=[500, 1_000, 2_000], fs=fs)
print("gain (dB) at 0.5, 1, 2 kHz:", np.round(20 * np.log10(np.abs(H)), 1))
```

The output is an apparent frequency of $3000$ Hz, and gains of $0$, $-6$ and $-65$ dB at 0.5, 1 and 2 kHz.

### 1.4 Linear time-invariant filters

::: def
[Definition 1.7 — LTI filter, impulse and frequency response]{.tag} A linear time-invariant (LTI) filter acts by convolution with its impulse response $h$:
$$
y[n] = (h * x)[n] = \sum_{m \in \mathbb Z} h[m]\, x[n - m].
$$

Complex exponentials are its eigenvectors: the input $e^{i\omega n}$ produces $H(e^{i\omega})\, e^{i\omega n}$, where the frequency response is
$$
H(e^{i\omega}) = \sum_m h[m]\, e^{-i\omega m}.
$$

A filter is FIR (finite impulse response) when $h$ has finitely many non-zero taps. It is IIR when it is defined by a recursion whose transfer function $H(z) = B(z)/A(z)$ has a non-trivial denominator.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.8 — BIBO stability]{.tag} An LTI filter maps every bounded input to a bounded output if and only if its impulse response is absolutely summable:
$$
\sum_m |h[m]| < \infty .
$$

::: proof
*Sufficiency.* If $|x[n]| \leq M$ for all $n$, then $|y[n]| \leq M \sum_m |h[m]|$.

*Necessity.* Take the bounded input $x[n] = \overline{h[-n]} / |h[-n]|$ where $h[-n] \neq 0$, and $0$ elsewhere. Then
$$
y[0] = \sum_m h[m]\, x[-m] = \sum_m |h[m]|,
$$
which must be finite. [∎]{.qed}
:::

FIR filters are therefore always stable. A causal IIR filter is stable if and only if all the poles of $H(z)$ lie strictly inside the unit circle.
::::

### 1.5 Designing a FIR filter

The ideal low-pass filter of cut-off $f_c$ has the impulse response $h_d[n] = (2 f_c / f_s)\, \mathrm{sinc}(2 f_c n / f_s)$: infinite and non-causal. The **window method** keeps $M$ central taps, multiplies them by a tapering window and delays the result by $(M-1)/2$ samples.

-   Symmetric taps give a **linear phase**: every frequency is delayed by the same $(M-1)/2$ samples, so pulse shapes are preserved — essential for radar and for transients.
-   The transition width shrinks like $1/M$; the window sets the stop-band attenuation (about $-53$ dB for Hamming).
-   Code 1.6 shows the result: $0$ dB in the pass band, $-6$ dB at the cut-off and $-65$ dB one octave above.

### 1.6 The matched filter and pulse compression

A receiver looks for a known waveform $s$ (a radar pulse, a pilot sequence) in white noise. Which linear filter makes the waveform stand out most?

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.9 — Matched filter]{.tag} Let $y = s + w$ with $s \in \mathbb C^N$ known and $w$ white noise of power $\sigma^2$. Among linear filters $h$, the output SNR at the decision time,
$$
\mathrm{SNR}(h) = \frac{|\langle s, h \rangle|^2}{\sigma^2\, \|h\|^2},
$$
is maximised by $h = s$ (up to a constant), that is, by correlating $y$ with the waveform. The maximum is the signal energy over the noise power:
$$
\mathrm{SNR}_{\max} = \frac{\|s\|^2}{\sigma^2}.
$$

::: proof
The filter output is the sum of a signal term and a noise term:
$$
\langle y, h \rangle = \langle s, h \rangle + \langle w, h \rangle .
$$

The noise term has variance $\sigma^2 \|h\|^2$, since the samples of $w$ are uncorrelated with power $\sigma^2$.

By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, $|\langle s, h \rangle|^2 \leq \|s\|^2 \|h\|^2$, with equality if and only if $h$ is proportional to $s$. Dividing by $\sigma^2 \|h\|^2$ gives the bound and the maximiser. [∎]{.qed}
:::

As a convolution, correlating with $s$ is filtering with the time-reversed conjugate $h[m] = \overline{s[N - 1 - m]}$, hence the name. The SNR gain over one sample of power $|s[n]|^2 = 1$ is $N$.
::::

A radar wants both a long pulse (energy, hence range) and a fine range resolution (a short pulse). **Pulse compression** reconciles them: transmit a long chirp of duration $T$ sweeping a band $B$, then apply the matched filter. The compressed pulse has a width of about $1/B$.

-   Sampled at its bandwidth, the chirp has $N = BT$ samples, so the matched filter gains $10 \log_{10}(BT)$ dB.
-   The range resolution is $c / (2B)$ instead of $cT/2$.
-   With $T = 50$ µs and $B = 4$ MHz: $BT = 200$, a gain of $23$ dB, and a resolution of $37.5$ m instead of $7.5$ km.

```python
# Code 1.10 — pulse compression of a linear FM chirp by the matched filter
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
B, T = 4e6, 50e-6                     # 4 MHz sweep, 50 us pulse
fs = B                                # complex baseband sampled at the bandwidth
N = int(round(B * T))                 # N = BT = 200 samples
t = np.arange(N) / fs
s = np.exp(1j * np.pi * (B / T) * (t - T / 2) ** 2)   # linear FM chirp, |s[n]| = 1
y = (rng.normal(size=2000) + 1j * rng.normal(size=2000)) / np.sqrt(2)  # noise, power 1
y[700:700 + N] += 0.25 * s            # echo at -12 dB per sample, delay 700
z = np.abs(np.correlate(y, s, mode="valid"))   # matched filter (s is conjugated)
print("estimated delay:", np.argmax(z))
print("output SNR (dB): %.1f" % (10 * np.log10(z.max() ** 2 / np.mean(z[:600] ** 2))))
print("predicted: -12 + 10 log10(BT) = %.1f dB" % (-12 + 10 * np.log10(B * T)))
```

The echo, invisible sample by sample at $-12$ dB, is found at the right delay ($700$) with an output SNR of about $10$ dB, close to the predicted $11$ dB.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 1
:::

-   Narrowband signals are processed as complex IQ samples of their envelope, at a rate set by the bandwidth, not the carrier.
-   Sampling at $f_s$ is lossless for spectra inside $(-f_s/2, f_s/2)$; outside, aliasing is irreversible.
-   The DFT has a bin spacing of $f_s/N$; windows trade main-lobe width for side-lobe level.
-   LTI filters are convolutions, diagonalised by complex exponentials; FIR filters are stable and can have linear phase.
-   The matched filter maximises the SNR by Cauchy–Schwarz; pulse compression turns $BT$ into a $10 \log_{10}(BT)$ dB gain.
::::

## 2. Time–frequency and time–scale representations {#ch2}

The DFT of a whole recording says which frequencies are present, not when. Speech, chirps, radar pulses and bearing impacts are non-stationary, so we need representations indexed by time *and* frequency. This chapter builds them, proves the limit on their resolution, and derives the speech features used in chapters 7 and 8.

### 2.1 Short-time Fourier transform and spectrogram

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — STFT and spectrogram]{.tag} Let $g$ be a window of length $L$ (Hann, Hamming…), $H$ a hop size and $N \geq L$ a DFT size. The short-time Fourier transform of $x$ is
$$
S_x[m, k] = \sum_{n} x[n]\, g[n - mH]\, e^{-2i\pi k (n - mH)/N},
$$
the DFT of the $m$-th windowed frame. The **spectrogram** is $|S_x[m, k]|^2$, an energy density on the time–frequency plane.
:::

The STFT is redundant when $H < L$, and it can be inverted.

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.2 — Overlap-add reconstruction]{.tag} Suppose the shifted windows sum to a constant (the COLA condition):
$$
\sum_{m} g[n - mH] = C \neq 0 \quad \text{for all } n .
$$
Then $x$ is recovered from its STFT by inverting each frame's DFT and adding the frames:
$$
x[n] = \frac1C \sum_m x[n]\, g[n - mH].
$$

::: proof
Since $N \geq L$, the inverse DFT of $S_x[m, \cdot]$ returns the windowed frame $x[n]\, g[n - mH]$ exactly. Summing over $m$ and using the COLA condition gives $C\, x[n]$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

The periodic Hann window with $H = L/2$ satisfies COLA with $C = 1$, which is why "Hann, 50 % overlap" is the default setting.
::::

### 2.2 The uncertainty principle

Short windows localise events in time but blur frequencies; long windows do the opposite. The trade-off is a theorem, not a weakness of the STFT.

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.3 — Heisenberg–Gabor uncertainty]{.tag} Let $g \in L^2(\mathbb R)$ with $\|g\| = 1$, centred in time and frequency. Define its spreads
$$
\sigma_t^2 = \int t^2 |g(t)|^2\, dt, \qquad \sigma_f^2 = \int f^2 |\hat g(f)|^2\, df .
$$
Then their product is bounded below, with equality exactly for Gaussian windows (up to translation and modulation):
$$
\sigma_t\, \sigma_f \geq \frac{1}{4\pi}.
$$

::: proof
*Sketch for smooth, fast-decaying $g$.* Integrate by parts:
$$
1 = \int |g|^2\, dt = -\int t\, \frac{d}{dt}|g(t)|^2\, dt = -2\, \mathrm{Re} \int t\, g(t)\, \overline{g'(t)}\, dt .
$$

By Cauchy–Schwarz, the right-hand side is at most $2\, \|t g\|\, \|g'\|$. By Plancherel, $g'$ has transform $2i\pi f \hat g(f)$, so $\|g'\| = 2\pi \sigma_f$, while $\|t g\| = \sigma_t$. Hence $1 \leq 4\pi \sigma_t \sigma_f$.

Equality in Cauchy–Schwarz forces $g' = -c\, t\, g$ with $c > 0$, whose solutions are the Gaussians. [∎]{.qed}
:::

A spectrogram cell therefore cannot be smaller than a fixed area. Gabor (1946) proposed to tile the plane with Gaussian-windowed atoms for this reason.
::::

::: ex
[Example 2.4 — Choosing the window]{.tag} For speech at $f_s = 16$ kHz:

-   a window of $32$ ms ($512$ samples) gives a bin spacing of $16000 / 512 = 31.25$ Hz, enough to resolve the harmonics of a $120$ Hz voice;
-   a window of $8$ ms ($128$ samples) gives $125$ Hz bins, which merge harmonics but localise a click to a few milliseconds.

Code 2.9 measures the same trade-off on a chirp with a click: the long window spreads the click over $128$ ms, the short one over $4$ ms.
:::

Quadratic distributions such as the Wigner–Ville distribution localise a single chirp perfectly, but create interference terms between components; Flandrin's book treats them (see References).

### 2.3 Wavelets and the scalogram

The STFT analyses all frequencies with the same window. Physical signals often call for a constant *relative* resolution instead: a 50 Hz hum needs fine frequency resolution, a 5 kHz impact needs fine time resolution.

::: def
[Definition 2.5 — Continuous wavelet transform, scalogram]{.tag} A wavelet $\psi \in L^2(\mathbb R)$ is admissible when
$$
C_\psi = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{|\hat\psi(f)|^2}{|f|}\, df < \infty,
$$
which forces $\hat \psi(0) = 0$: a wavelet has zero mean. The continuous wavelet transform at scale $a > 0$ and time $b$ is
$$
W_x(a, b) = \int x(t)\, \frac{1}{\sqrt a}\, \overline{\psi\Big(\frac{t - b}{a}\Big)}\, dt,
$$
and the **scalogram** is $|W_x(a, b)|^2$.
:::

-   If $\psi$ has centre frequency $f_0$ and bandwidth $\Delta f$, the wavelet dilated by $a$ has centre $f_0 / a$ and bandwidth $\Delta f / a$. The relative bandwidth is constant: a **constant-Q** analysis.
-   The **Morlet wavelet**, a Gaussian-windowed complex exponential, is the usual choice for time–frequency maps:
$$
\psi(t) = \pi^{-1/4}\, e^{i \omega_0 t}\, e^{-t^2/2}, \qquad \omega_0 \approx 6 .
$$
-   When $C_\psi < \infty$, $x$ can be reconstructed from $W_x$ (Calderón's formula; see Mallat's book in the References).

### 2.4 Discrete wavelets and filter banks

Sampling scales on a dyadic grid $a = 2^j$ leads to a fast, non-redundant transform implemented by a cascade of two-channel filter banks.

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.6 — The Haar filter bank is orthogonal]{.tag} For $x \in \mathbb R^{2K}$, define the approximation and detail coefficients
$$
a_k = \frac{x_{2k} + x_{2k+1}}{\sqrt 2}, \qquad d_k = \frac{x_{2k} - x_{2k+1}}{\sqrt 2}.
$$
The map $x \mapsto (a, d)$ is orthogonal: it preserves energy and is inverted by its transpose.

::: proof
The map acts independently on each pair $(x_{2k}, x_{2k+1})$ through the matrix
$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt 2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix},
$$
whose rows are orthonormal. A block-diagonal matrix with orthogonal blocks is orthogonal. [∎]{.qed}
:::

Iterating on the approximation $a$ gives the discrete wavelet transform. Its cost is $N + N/2 + N/4 + \dots < 2N$ operations, linear in $N$, better than the FFT.
::::

Daubechies wavelets replace the Haar pair by longer filters with more vanishing moments, so that smooth pieces of a signal produce small details. Thresholding small details then denoises: Donoho and Johnstone (1994) proved near-optimality of soft thresholding at $\sigma \sqrt{2 \log N}$.

### 2.5 Perceptual features: mel spectrum, cepstrum and MFCC

Speech and audio systems compress the spectrogram along a perceptual frequency axis and separate the source from the filter.

::: def
[Definition 2.7 — Mel scale and MFCC]{.tag} The mel scale maps a frequency in hertz to a perceived pitch:
$$
m(f) = 2595 \log_{10}\Big(1 + \frac{f}{700}\Big).
$$

The MFCC of a frame (Davis and Mermelstein, 1980) are computed in four steps:

1.  the power spectrum of the windowed frame;
2.  energies in $20$–$40$ triangular filters equally spaced in mel;
3.  the logarithm of each energy;
4.  a discrete cosine transform, keeping the first $12$ or $13$ coefficients.
:::

The logarithm in step 3 is not cosmetic.

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.8 — The cepstrum turns convolution into a sum]{.tag} If $s = e * h$, then at every frequency where the spectra do not vanish:
$$
\log |S(f)| = \log |E(f)| + \log |H(f)|.
$$
Any linear map of the log-spectrum, such as the DCT of the MFCC or the inverse Fourier transform of the real cepstrum, separates the two contributions additively.

::: proof
The Fourier transform of a convolution is the product $S = E \cdot H$, and the logarithm of a product of moduli is the sum of the logarithms. [∎]{.qed}
:::

For voiced speech, $e$ is a pulse train at the pitch $F_0$ and $h$ the smooth vocal-tract response (ch. 7.2). In the cepstrum, $h$ occupies the low quefrencies and $e$ a peak at the pitch period. A pitch of 125 Hz gives a peak at 8 ms, that is 128 samples at 16 kHz.
::::

::: ex
[Example 2.9 — Spectrogram versus scalogram on a chirp with a click]{.tag} The code compares two Hann windows on a linear chirp from $100$ Hz to $3$ kHz with a $1$ ms click at $t = 1$ s, then computes a Morlet scalogram in the Fourier domain.
:::

```python
# Code 2.9 — the time-frequency trade-off, and a Morlet scalogram
import numpy as np
from scipy import signal

fs = 8_000
t = np.arange(2 * fs) / fs                       # 2 s
x = signal.chirp(t, f0=100, t1=2, f1=3_000)      # linear chirp 100 Hz -> 3 kHz
x[8_000:8_008] += 5.0                            # a 1 ms click at t = 1 s

for L in (64, 1024):                             # short and long Hann windows
    f, tt, S = signal.stft(x, fs, window="hann", nperseg=L, noverlap=L // 2)
    P = np.abs(S) ** 2
    k = np.argmin(np.abs(tt - 0.5))              # frame closest to t = 0.5 s
    width = np.sum(P[:, k] > 0.5 * P[:, k].max()) * fs / L
    hf = P[f > 3_500].sum(axis=0)                # energy above the chirp band
    spread = np.sum(hf > 0.1 * hf.max()) * (L / 2) / fs * 1e3
    print(f"L={L:4d}: ridge {f[np.argmax(P[:, k])]:6.1f} Hz, -3 dB width {width:5.1f} Hz,"
          f" click spread over {spread:5.1f} ms")

def morlet_cwt(x, fs, freqs, w0=6.0):
    """CWT with an analytic Morlet wavelet, computed in the Fourier domain."""
    X = np.fft.fft(x)
    om = 2 * np.pi * np.fft.fftfreq(len(x), 1 / fs)    # angular frequencies
    W = np.empty((len(freqs), len(x)), complex)
    for i, fc in enumerate(freqs):
        a = w0 / (2 * np.pi * fc)                # scale whose centre frequency is fc
        psi_hat = np.pi ** -0.25 * np.exp(-0.5 * (a * om - w0) ** 2) * (om > 0)
        W[i] = np.fft.ifft(X * np.sqrt(a) * psi_hat)
    return W

freqs = np.geomspace(100, 3_500, 48)             # constant-Q grid of centre frequencies
W = np.abs(morlet_cwt(x, fs, freqs)) ** 2
print("scalogram ridge at t = 0.5 s: %.0f Hz (true 825 Hz)" % freqs[np.argmax(W[:, 4_000])])
```

Typical output:

-   with $L = 64$, the ridge at $t = 0.5$ s is $250$ Hz wide and the click spreads over $4$ ms;
-   with $L = 1024$, the ridge is $70$ Hz wide — the chirp moves by about $185$ Hz inside one $128$ ms window — and the click spreads over $128$ ms;
-   the scalogram ridge lies at $832$ Hz for a true instantaneous frequency of $825$ Hz.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 2
:::

-   The spectrogram is the squared modulus of windowed DFTs; with a COLA window the STFT is exactly invertible.
-   The uncertainty principle bounds the product of time and frequency spreads by $1/(4\pi)$, reached by Gaussian windows.
-   Wavelets give a constant-Q analysis: fine time resolution at high frequency, fine frequency resolution at low frequency.
-   The discrete wavelet transform is an orthogonal filter bank computed in linear time.
-   MFCC = mel energies, logarithm, DCT; the logarithm turns the source–filter convolution into a sum.
::::

## 3. The machine-learning toolbox: classification, clustering, optimisation {#ch3}

Before deep networks, a signal is usually summarised by a few hand-crafted features — energy, kurtosis, spectral centroid — and fed to a standard learner. This chapter states what such a learner estimates, reviews the main families of classifiers and clustering algorithms, and proves the convergence rate of gradient descent, the engine of everything in chapter 4.

### 3.1 Supervised learning and the Bayes rule

Data are pairs $(x_i, y_i)$, drawn independently from an unknown distribution $P$ on features $x$ and labels $y \in \{1, \dots, K\}$. A classifier $f$ is judged by its risk $R(f) = P(f(x) \neq y)$, and learning minimises an empirical estimate of it over a class of functions.

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.1 — The Bayes classifier]{.tag} The classifier that picks the most probable label given the observation,
$$
f^\star(x) = \arg\max_{k}\ P(y = k \mid x),
$$
has the smallest risk among all classifiers.

::: proof
For any $f$, condition on $x$: the probability of error given $x$ is $1 - P(y = f(x) \mid x)$.

It is minimised, for each observation separately, by choosing the label with the largest conditional probability. Integrating over $x$ preserves the inequality. [∎]{.qed}
:::

With two classes, $f^\star$ compares the likelihood ratio $p(x \mid 1) / p(x \mid 0)$ with the threshold $P(y = 0) / P(y = 1)$: the detection tests of ch. 5 are Bayes rules with a threshold set differently.
::::

**Unsupervised** learning has no labels: it looks for structure — clusters, low-dimensional subspaces, densities — in the $x_i$ alone. Industrial data are often unlabelled or labelled only for rare events, so both settings appear in every use case.

::: note
[Note 3.2 — Splitting signal data without leakage]{.tag} Consecutive windows of one recording are strongly correlated. If windows of the same recording, speaker, device or machine land in both the training and the test set, the test score measures memorisation of that source, not generalisation.

-   Split by *source*: recording, session, speaker, emitter, machine or day.
-   Fit normalisations (means, variances, PCA) on the training set only.
-   Keep a final test set untouched until the end.
:::

### 3.2 The main families of classifiers

::: def
[Definition 3.3 — Linear classifiers: logistic regression and SVM]{.tag} Both predict with the sign of a score $w^\top x + b$ (one score per class for $K > 2$) and differ by their loss.

-   **Logistic regression** models $P(y = 1 \mid x) = \sigma(w^\top x + b)$, with $\sigma(u) = 1/(1 + e^{-u})$, and minimises the convex cross-entropy loss.
-   The **support vector machine** minimises the hinge loss plus $\lambda \|w\|^2$, which maximises the margin between classes. With a kernel $k(x, x')$, such as the Gaussian kernel, it separates classes with non-linear boundaries.
:::

| Family | Principle | Strength on signal features | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| Linear models (logistic, linear SVM) | weighted sum of features | fast, calibrated scores, interpretable weights | only linear boundaries in the chosen features |
| Kernel SVM | linear in a feature space defined by a kernel | strong on small data sets | quadratic cost in the number of examples |
| $k$-nearest neighbours | vote of the closest training points | no training; asymptotic error at most twice the Bayes error (Cover and Hart, 1967) | needs a good distance; slow at test time |
| Decision trees, random forests, gradient boosting | axis-aligned splits, averaged or boosted | robust to feature scales, handle heterogeneous indicators | no notion of time or frequency structure |
| Neural networks (ch. 4) | learned features and classifier | work on raw signals | need data and compute |

### 3.3 Unsupervised learning: clustering

Clustering partitions $n$ points into groups. Three algorithms cover most industrial needs.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.4 — Lloyd's algorithm for k-means]{.tag} The k-means objective of an assignment $c$ and centres $\mu_1, \dots, \mu_K$ is
$$
J(c, \mu) = \sum_{i=1}^n \|x_i - \mu_{c(i)}\|^2 .
$$
Lloyd's algorithm alternates two steps: assign each point to its nearest centre, then move each centre to the mean of its points. $J$ never increases, and the algorithm stops after finitely many iterations.

::: proof
The assignment step minimises $J$ over $c$ for fixed $\mu$, since each term is minimised separately. The update step minimises $J$ over the centres for a fixed assignment, since the mean minimises a sum of squared distances. Each step can only lower the objective.

There are finitely many assignments, and an assignment cannot repeat once $J$ strictly decreases (ties broken consistently), so the algorithm terminates. [∎]{.qed}
:::

The limit is a local minimum only: practice restarts from several initialisations (k-means++). k-means assumes round clusters of similar sizes and a known $K$.
::::

::: def
[Definition 3.5 — Gaussian mixtures and the EM algorithm]{.tag} A Gaussian mixture has density
$$
p(x) = \sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k\, \mathcal N(x; \mu_k, \Sigma_k).
$$

EM (Dempster, Laird and Rubin, 1977) alternates two steps.

-   **E-step**: compute the responsibilities $r_{ik} = P(k \mid x_i)$ under the current parameters.
-   **M-step**: re-estimate $\pi_k$, $\mu_k$ and $\Sigma_k$ as responsibility-weighted frequencies, means and covariances.

Each iteration does not decrease the log-likelihood, because the E-step makes a lower bound (Jensen's inequality) tight and the M-step maximises it. Mixtures give soft assignments and elliptical clusters; they model MFCC frames in speaker recognition (ch. 7.3).
:::

::: def
[Definition 3.6 — DBSCAN]{.tag} Given a radius $\varepsilon$ and an integer $m$, a point is a **core point** if at least $m$ points lie within distance $\varepsilon$ of it. Clusters are the sets of points reachable from one another through chains of core points; points reachable from no core point are labelled **noise**.

DBSCAN (Ester, Kriegel, Sander and Xu, 1996) needs no number of clusters, finds clusters of any shape and isolates outliers — three properties that radar deinterleaving needs (ch. 6.3). Its weakness is a single density scale $\varepsilon$, so features must be standardised first.
:::

Hierarchical (agglomerative) clustering with Ward's criterion and principal component analysis (PCA) complete the toolbox: the first builds a tree of nested partitions, the second projects data on the eigenvectors of the covariance with the largest eigenvalues (used for anomaly detection in ch. 9.4).

### 3.4 Evaluation

::: def
[Definition 3.7 — Detection and clustering metrics]{.tag}

-   For a binary detector with a threshold, the **probability of false alarm** $P_{FA}$ is the rate of positives on negative examples, and the **probability of detection** $P_D$ (recall) is the rate of positives on positive examples.
-   The **ROC curve** traces $P_D$ against $P_{FA}$ as the threshold varies; its area (AUC) is the probability that a random positive scores above a random negative.
-   The **equal error rate** (EER) is the error where false acceptances and false rejections are equal, the standard metric of speaker verification (ch. 7.1).
-   **Precision** is the fraction of true positives among detections; F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall.
-   For clustering, the **adjusted Rand index** (ARI) measures the agreement of two partitions, corrected for chance: 1 for identical partitions, about 0 for random ones.
:::

::: ex
[Example 3.8 — Accuracy under class imbalance]{.tag} A fleet of pumps produces 10 000 windows, of which 100 precede a failure.

-   The classifier "always healthy" has an accuracy of 99 % and a recall of 0.
-   A detector that flags 150 windows, 80 of them before failures, has a recall of 0.80 and a precision of 0.53.
-   Its F1 score is
$$
F_1 = \frac{2 \times 0.53 \times 0.80}{0.53 + 0.80} \approx 0.64 .
$$

Predictive maintenance (ch. 9) is always judged on recall, precision and the cost of each error, never on accuracy.
:::

### 3.5 Optimisation and gradient descent

Training minimises an empirical loss $F(\theta)$. Gradient descent iterates $\theta_{k+1} = \theta_k - \eta\, \nabla F(\theta_k)$ with a step size $\eta$.

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.9 — Rate of gradient descent on smooth convex functions]{.tag} Let $F$ be convex with an $L$-Lipschitz gradient, and let $\theta^\star$ be a minimiser. With the step $\eta = 1/L$, the iterates satisfy, for every $k \geq 1$:
$$
F(\theta_k) - F(\theta^\star) \leq \frac{L\, \|\theta_0 - \theta^\star\|^2}{2k}.
$$

::: proof
Write $g_k = \nabla F(\theta_k)$.

1.  *Descent lemma.* The Lipschitz gradient gives $F(\theta_{k+1}) \leq F(\theta_k) - \|g_k\|^2 / (2L)$: the values decrease.
2.  *Convexity.* The gap is bounded by a linear term:
$$
F(\theta_k) - F(\theta^\star) \leq \langle g_k, \theta_k - \theta^\star \rangle .
$$
3.  *Expanding the square* of $\|\theta_{k+1} - \theta^\star\|$, where $\theta_{k+1} = \theta_k - g_k / L$:
$$
\langle g_k, \theta_k - \theta^\star \rangle - \frac{\|g_k\|^2}{2L} = \frac{L}{2}\big(\|\theta_k - \theta^\star\|^2 - \|\theta_{k+1} - \theta^\star\|^2\big).
$$
4.  Combining 1–3, $F(\theta_{k+1}) - F(\theta^\star)$ is bounded by the right-hand side of step 3. Summing from $0$ to $k - 1$, the sum telescopes and is at most $L \|\theta_0 - \theta^\star\|^2 / 2$.
5.  The values decrease (step 1), so $k$ times the last gap is at most this sum. [∎]{.qed}
:::

The rate $1/k$ is slow; strong convexity gives a geometric rate, and Nesterov's acceleration gives $1/k^2$ (see [Convex Optimization and Applications in Machine Learning](../s1-convex-optimization/index.html)).
::::

Deep networks are not convex, and their losses are sums over millions of examples. **Stochastic gradient descent** replaces $\nabla F$ by the gradient on a random mini-batch, an unbiased estimate; momentum and Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2015) rescale the steps per parameter. On non-convex losses, the guarantees concern convergence to stationary points, not to global minima.

The code below runs the classical chain on synthetic signals of three kinds — a tone, a square wave and sparse impulses, all in strong noise. Four features are fed to two classifiers, and the same features to k-means.

```python
# Code 3.10 — hand-crafted features, two classifiers and k-means
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, adjusted_rand_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
fs, n = 1_000, 512

def make(label):
    t = np.arange(n) / fs
    f0 = rng.uniform(20, 120)
    if label == 0:                                   # tone
        x = np.sin(2 * np.pi * f0 * t + rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi))
    elif label == 1:                                 # square wave (odd harmonics)
        x = np.sign(np.sin(2 * np.pi * f0 * t))
    else:                                            # sparse impulses (a "fault")
        x = (rng.random(n) < 0.02) * rng.normal(0, 3, n)
    return x + rng.normal(0, 1.5, n)

def features(x):
    P = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x)) ** 2
    f = np.fft.rfftfreq(n, 1 / fs)
    return [np.sqrt(np.mean(x ** 2)),               # RMS
            stats.kurtosis(x, fisher=False),        # kurtosis (3 for a Gaussian)
            (f * P).sum() / P.sum(),                # spectral centroid
            np.mean(np.diff(np.sign(x)) != 0)]      # zero-crossing rate

y = rng.integers(0, 3, 900)
F = np.array([features(make(c)) for c in y])
Ftr, Fte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(F, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)
scaler = StandardScaler().fit(Ftr)                  # fitted on the training set only
Ftr, Fte = scaler.transform(Ftr), scaler.transform(Fte)
for clf in (LogisticRegression(max_iter=1_000), RandomForestClassifier(random_state=0)):
    acc = accuracy_score(yte, clf.fit(Ftr, ytr).predict(Fte))
    print(f"{type(clf).__name__:24s} test accuracy {acc:.3f}")
km = KMeans(n_clusters=3, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit(scaler.transform(F))
print("k-means ARI (no labels used):", round(adjusted_rand_score(y, km.labels_), 3))
```

Expected output: test accuracies of about $0.95$ (logistic regression) and $0.93$ (random forest), and an ARI of about $0.75$ for k-means. Four well-chosen features almost solve the task; chapter 4 asks whether a network can find such features alone.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 3
:::

-   The Bayes classifier maximises the posterior probability; with two classes it is a likelihood-ratio test.
-   Split signal data by source (recording, speaker, device, machine), never by window.
-   Linear models, kernels, nearest neighbours and tree ensembles are strong baselines on hand-crafted features.
-   k-means decreases its objective monotonically; EM does the same for the likelihood of a mixture; DBSCAN finds an unknown number of clusters and flags noise.
-   Judge detectors with ROC, EER, precision and recall, not accuracy.
-   Gradient descent with step $1/L$ converges at rate $1/k$ on smooth convex losses.
::::

## 4. Deep learning: basics and main architectures {#ch4}

A deep network learns the features and the classifier together, from raw samples or spectrograms. This chapter defines the building blocks, shows that a convolutional layer is a learnable filter bank, explains why recurrent networks forget, and ends with a first, proven answer to the course's question: what does depth add?

### 4.1 Multilayer perceptrons

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Multilayer perceptron]{.tag} A multilayer perceptron (MLP) of depth $L$ alternates affine maps and a pointwise non-linearity $\sigma$ (ReLU $\sigma(u) = \max(u, 0)$, tanh…):
$$
h_0 = x, \qquad z_\ell = W_\ell\, h_{\ell - 1} + b_\ell, \qquad h_\ell = \sigma(z_\ell) \quad (\ell < L),
$$
and the last pre-activation $z_L$ gives the output. For classification, a softmax turns $z_L$ into probabilities $p_k = e^{z_{L,k}} / \sum_j e^{z_{L,j}}$, trained with the cross-entropy loss $-\log p_y$.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 4.2 — Universal approximation]{.tag} Let $\sigma$ be continuous and not a polynomial. For every continuous function $f$ on a compact set $K \subset \mathbb R^d$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$, there is a network with *one* hidden layer such that
$$
\sup_{x \in K} |f(x) - g(x)| \leq \varepsilon .
$$

Proofs: Cybenko (1989) for sigmoids, Hornik (1991), and Leshno, Lin, Pinkus and Schocken (1993) for every non-polynomial activation.
:::

The theorem says nothing about the *number* of hidden units needed. Section 4.7 shows that this number can be exponentially larger for a shallow network than for a deep one.

### 4.2 Backpropagation

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.3 — Backpropagation for an MLP]{.tag} For one example with label $y$ and loss $\ell = -\log p_y$, define $\delta_\ell = \partial \ell / \partial z_\ell$. Then, with $e_y$ the one-hot vector of $y$:
$$
\delta_L = p - e_y, \qquad \delta_\ell = \big(W_{\ell+1}^\top\, \delta_{\ell+1}\big) \odot \sigma'(z_\ell),
$$
$$
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial W_\ell} = \delta_\ell\, h_{\ell-1}^\top, \qquad \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial b_\ell} = \delta_\ell .
$$
All gradients cost about twice the forward pass.

::: proof
*Output.* Since $\ell = -z_{L,y} + \log \sum_j e^{z_{L,j}}$, its derivative in $z_{L,j}$ is $-\mathbb 1[j = y] + p_j$.

*Recursion.* $z_{\ell+1}$ depends on $z_\ell$ through $W_{\ell+1} \sigma(z_\ell)$, whose Jacobian is $W_{\ell+1}\, \mathrm{diag}(\sigma'(z_\ell))$. The chain rule (Definition 0.5) transposes it.

*Weights.* $z_\ell$ is linear in $W_\ell$ with coefficient $h_{\ell-1}$.

*Cost.* Each backward step is one product by a transposed matrix and one pointwise product — the same sizes as the forward step. [∎]{.qed}
:::

Automatic differentiation in PyTorch applies the same reverse-mode rule to any composition of differentiable operations (Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams, 1986, popularised it for networks).
::::

### 4.3 Convolutional networks: learnable filter banks

::: def
[Definition 4.4 — One-dimensional convolutional layer]{.tag} A layer with $C$ input channels, $C'$ output channels, kernel size $K$ and dilation $d$ computes, for each output channel $c$:
$$
y_c[n] = \sigma\Big(b_c + \sum_{c'=1}^{C} \sum_{m=0}^{K-1} w_{c,c'}[m]\, x_{c'}[n + m d]\Big).
$$
Each output channel is a sum of FIR filters (Definition 1.7) followed by a non-linearity. The number of parameters, $C C' K + C'$, does not depend on the length of the signal.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.5 — Equivariance, invariance and receptive field]{.tag} Let $T_\tau$ shift a signal, $(T_\tau x)[n] = x[n - \tau]$. Ignoring borders:

1.  a stride-1 convolutional layer commutes with shifts: $\mathrm{Layer}(T_\tau x) = T_\tau\, \mathrm{Layer}(x)$;
2.  a stack of such layers followed by a global average over time is shift-invariant;
3.  a stack of $L$ layers with kernel size $K$ and dilations $d_1, \dots, d_L$ sees a window of input samples of length
$$
R = 1 + (K - 1) \sum_{\ell=1}^{L} d_\ell .
$$

::: proof
1.  Replace $x$ by $T_\tau x$ in Definition 4.4: the inner sum becomes the original one evaluated at $n - \tau$. The pointwise non-linearity commutes with shifts.
2.  Compositions of shift-commuting maps commute with shifts, and the average over all $n$ of a shifted sequence equals the average of the sequence.
3.  One layer makes each output depend on the inputs $n, n + d, \dots, n + (K-1)d$: the window grows by $(K - 1) d_\ell$ samples per layer. [∎]{.qed}
:::

Strides and pooling keep equivariance only for shifts that are multiples of the stride. Doubling dilations make the receptive field grow exponentially with depth (WaveNet): with $K = 3$ and dilations $1, 2, 4, \dots, 512$ (10 layers), $R = 1 + 2 \times 1023 = 2047$ samples.
::::

On spectrograms, two-dimensional convolutions treat the time–frequency image like a picture; shift equivariance along the mel axis then approximates invariance to small pitch changes.

### 4.4 Recurrent networks and long dependencies

A recurrent network reads a sequence $x_1, \dots, x_T$ and updates a state $h_t = \tanh(W h_{t-1} + U x_t + b)$. Training unrolls it in time and backpropagates through the unrolled graph.

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.6 — Vanishing gradients]{.tag} If the spectral norm of the recurrent matrix satisfies $\|W\|_2 \leq \gamma < 1$, then the gradient of the state at time $T$ with respect to the state at an earlier time $t$ decays geometrically:
$$
\Big\| \frac{\partial h_T}{\partial h_t} \Big\|_2 \leq \gamma^{\,T - t}.
$$

::: proof
By the chain rule, the Jacobian is the product of $T - t$ factors $\mathrm{diag}(\tanh'(a_s))\, W$, where $a_s$ is the pre-activation. Each factor has norm at most $\gamma$ because $|\tanh'| \leq 1$, and operator norms are sub-multiplicative. [∎]{.qed}
:::

With $\|W\|_2 > 1$ the product can instead explode. The LSTM (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997) adds a cell state updated additively, $c_t = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot \tilde c_t$, whose Jacobian along the cell path is the learned forget gate $\mathrm{diag}(f_t)$: the network decides how long to remember.
::::

### 4.5 Autoencoders, attention and transformers

::: def
[Definition 4.7 — Autoencoder and denoising autoencoder]{.tag} An autoencoder is an encoder $E$ and a decoder $D$ trained to minimise $\|x - D(E(x))\|^2$ through a narrow code $E(x)$. A **denoising** autoencoder (Vincent, Larochelle, Bengio and Manzagol, 2008) is trained to output the clean $x$ from a corrupted input, minimising $\|x - D(E(\tilde x))\|^2$.

A linear autoencoder trained with the squared error spans the principal subspace of PCA (Baldi and Hornik, 1989). Autoencoders serve as anomaly detectors (ch. 9.4) and as restoration networks (ch. 8.5).
:::

::: def
[Definition 4.8 — Self-attention]{.tag} Let $X \in \mathbb R^{T \times d}$ hold $T$ tokens (audio frames, radar pulses) as rows. With learned matrices, set $Q = X W_Q$, $K = X W_K$ and $V = X W_V$. Self-attention outputs
$$
\mathrm{Attn}(X) = \mathrm{softmax}\Big(\frac{Q K^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\Big)\, V,
$$
where the softmax acts on each row. A transformer block (Vaswani et al., 2017) chains several attention heads and an MLP, each wrapped in a residual connection and a normalisation.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.9 — Attention ignores order]{.tag} For every permutation matrix $\Pi$:
$$
\mathrm{Attn}(\Pi X) = \Pi\, \mathrm{Attn}(X).
$$

::: proof
Permuting the rows of $X$ permutes the rows of the queries, keys and values, so the score matrix becomes $\Pi Q K^\top \Pi^\top$. A row-wise softmax commutes with a simultaneous permutation of rows and columns. Multiplying by the permuted values $\Pi V$ cancels the factor $\Pi^\top \Pi = I$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

Order must therefore be injected, through positional encodings or, for radar pulses, through the times of arrival themselves.
::::

### 4.6 Training in practice

::: note
[Note 4.10 — A training recipe for signals]{.tag}

-   **Architecture**: residual connections (He et al., 2016) and batch normalisation make deep stacks trainable; initialise ReLU layers with variance $2 / \text{fan-in}$.
-   **Optimisation**: Adam or SGD with momentum, a learning-rate schedule, early stopping on a validation set split by source (Note 3.2).
-   **Regularisation**: weight decay, dropout, and above all **data augmentation** that respects the physics — random time shifts, gains, added noise at random SNR, small carrier offsets for radio, time and frequency masking of spectrograms (SpecAugment, Park et al., 2019).
-   **Diagnosis**: compare with the classical chain of the same chapter; a network that loses to four hand-crafted features needs more data, more training or a better input representation.
:::

The code below trains a small 1D CNN on the raw signals of Code 3.10, with no hand-crafted features.

```python
# Code 4.11 — a 1D CNN learns its own filter bank on raw signals
import numpy as np
import torch
from torch import nn

torch.manual_seed(0)
torch.set_num_threads(1)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, fs = 512, 1_000

def batch(m):
    """Tone / square wave / sparse impulses in strong noise, random phase and pitch."""
    y = rng.integers(0, 3, m)
    t = np.arange(n) / fs
    f0 = rng.uniform(20, 120, (m, 1))
    ph = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, (m, 1))
    tone = np.sin(2 * np.pi * f0 * t + ph)
    square = np.sign(tone)
    imp = (rng.random((m, n)) < 0.02) * rng.normal(0, 3, (m, n))
    x = np.choose(y[:, None], [tone, square, imp]) + rng.normal(0, 1.5, (m, n))
    return torch.tensor(x[:, None, :], dtype=torch.float32), torch.tensor(y)

net = nn.Sequential(                       # a learnable filter bank, then invariance
    nn.Conv1d(1, 16, kernel_size=33, padding=16), nn.BatchNorm1d(16), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool1d(4),
    nn.Conv1d(16, 32, kernel_size=9, padding=4), nn.BatchNorm1d(32), nn.ReLU(),
    nn.AdaptiveAvgPool1d(1), nn.Flatten(),  # global average pooling: shift invariance
    nn.Linear(32, 3))
opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr=3e-3)
for step in range(250):
    x, y = batch(64)
    loss = nn.functional.cross_entropy(net(x), y)
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
x, y = batch(1_000)
net.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    acc = (net(x).argmax(1) == y).float().mean().item()
print(f"test accuracy {acc:.3f}, parameters {sum(p.numel() for p in net.parameters())}")
```

With about 5 400 parameters and 16 000 training signals, the network reaches a test accuracy of about $0.91$, below the $0.95$ of the four features of Code 3.10. It had to discover kurtosis-like and harmonic detectors from data alone. Exercise 8 asks whether longer training closes the gap; on problems where nobody knows the right features, this discovery is the whole point.

### 4.7 What makes deep learning deep? A first answer

The universal approximation theorem allows one hidden layer; the question is how many units it needs. The following example, due to Telgarsky (2016), shows a function that a narrow deep network computes exactly and that every shallow network of sub-exponential width misses.

:::: prop
[Lemma 4.12 — Shallow ReLU networks have few pieces]{.tag} A one-hidden-layer ReLU network with $m$ units, from $\mathbb R$ to $\mathbb R$, is continuous and piecewise affine with at most $m + 1$ pieces.

::: proof
It is a constant plus a sum of terms $a_j \max(w_j x + b_j, 0)$. Each term is affine except at the single point $-b_j / w_j$, so the sum has at most $m$ breakpoints. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.13 — Depth separation (after Telgarsky, 2016)]{.tag} Let $\tau^k$ be the $k$-fold composition of the tent map on $[0, 1]$, written with two ReLU units:
$$
\tau(x) = 2\,\mathrm{ReLU}(x) - 4\,\mathrm{ReLU}(x - 1/2).
$$

1.  $\tau^k$ is computed exactly by a ReLU network of depth $k$ with $2$ units per layer, and it has $2^k$ affine pieces.
2.  Every continuous piecewise affine $g$ with at most $p$ pieces on $[0, 1]$ satisfies
$$
\int_0^1 |\tau^k(x) - g(x)|\, dx \geq \frac18 - \frac{p + 1}{2^{k+2}} .
$$
3.  Hence a one-hidden-layer ReLU network with at most $2^{k-2} - 2$ units has an $L^1$ error of at least $1/16$.

::: proof
*Sketch, in five steps.*

1.  The tent map sends the unit interval onto itself with two affine pieces. By induction, each of the $2^{k-1}$ pieces of $\tau^{k-1}$ maps its interval affinely onto the unit interval, and $\tau$ splits it in two. This gives $2^k$ pieces, forming $2^{k-1}$ teeth.
2.  The graph of $\tau^k$ crosses the level $1/2$ twice per tooth. Between consecutive crossings lie $2^k - 1$ triangles of base $2^{-k}$ and height $1/2$, alternately above and below the level, each of area $2^{-k-2}$.
3.  Since $g$ is continuous with $p$ affine pieces, $g - 1/2$ changes sign at most $p$ times. At most $p$ triangle bases contain a sign change. The others form at most $p + 1$ runs of consecutive triangles on which this sign is constant.
4.  Triangles alternate, so in a run of $r$ triangles at least $\lfloor r/2 \rfloor$ lie on the wrong side of $1/2$ relative to $g$. There, $|\tau^k - g| \geq |\tau^k - 1/2|$, which integrates to the triangle's area.
5.  Summing over runs, with $\lfloor r/2 \rfloor \geq (r - 1)/2$, at least $2^{k-1} - 1 - p$ triangles are wrong. Multiplying by $2^{-k-2}$ gives item 2; Lemma 4.12 with $p \leq m + 1$ gives item 3. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: key
[Key result — depth buys exponentially many linear regions]{.tag}
$$
\text{depth } k,\ 2k \text{ units} \ \longrightarrow\ 2^k \text{ pieces}, \qquad \text{depth } 2 \ \longrightarrow\ \text{width} \geq 2^{k-2} - 1 \text{ to approximate}
$$
:::

```python
# Code 4.14 — counting the linear pieces of a deep, narrow ReLU network
import numpy as np

relu = lambda z: np.maximum(z, 0.0)
tent = lambda z: 2 * relu(z) - 4 * relu(z - 0.5)      # one layer with two ReLU units
x = np.linspace(0, 1, 2 ** 12 + 1)
y = x.copy()
for k in range(1, 7):
    y = tent(y)                                       # depth k, width 2
    slopes = np.diff(y) / np.diff(x)
    pieces = 1 + np.count_nonzero(np.abs(np.diff(slopes)) > 1e-6)
    print(f"depth {k}: {pieces:3d} linear pieces with {2 * k:2d} ReLU units;"
          f" an exact one-hidden-layer copy needs at least {pieces - 1} units")
```

At depth 6, twelve units produce 64 pieces; an exact shallow copy needs 63 units. Composition reuses the same folds at every scale, the way a signal is built of samples, periods, phonemes and words. Chapter 10 completes this answer with invariance and stability.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 4
:::

-   An MLP alternates affine maps and non-linearities; one hidden layer approximates any continuous function, at an unspecified width.
-   Backpropagation is the chain rule in reverse order; its cost is a small multiple of the forward pass.
-   A convolutional layer is a learnable FIR filter bank; it is shift-equivariant, and global pooling makes it shift-invariant.
-   Plain recurrent networks forget geometrically; LSTM gates create an additive memory path.
-   Attention is permutation-equivariant: order must be injected.
-   Depth can be exponentially more efficient than width: $\tau^k$ needs $2k$ units deep and about $2^{k-2}$ units shallow.
::::

## 5. Use case: signal detection for cognitive radio {#ch5}

A cognitive radio (Mitola and Maguire, 1999; Haykin, 2005) transmits in licensed bands when, and only when, their owners are silent. It must decide from a few milliseconds of samples whether a band is occupied — a detection problem at negative SNR. This chapter solves it optimally under a physical model, finds the limit of that solution, and asks what learning adds.

### 5.1 Operational context and physical model

Licensed spectrum is often idle at a given place and time. A *secondary* user senses a band, transmits in a *spectrum hole*, and leaves as soon as the *primary* user returns; IEEE 802.22, for instance, standardises this access in television bands. Sensing must work far below 0 dB: the secondary receiver may sit in a fade or behind an obstacle while a primary receiver nearby still needs protection (the hidden-terminal problem).

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — Spectrum sensing as a binary test]{.tag} From $N$ complex baseband samples, decide between
$$
\mathcal H_0 : y[n] = w[n], \qquad \mathcal H_1 : y[n] = h\, s[n] + w[n],
$$
where $w$ is white Gaussian noise of power $\sigma^2$, $s$ the primary signal and $h$ the channel gain. The per-sample SNR is $\gamma = |h|^2 P_s / \sigma^2$.

A detector is judged by its false-alarm probability $P_{FA}$, which measures lost opportunities, and its detection probability $P_D$, which measures the protection of the primary user.
:::

### 5.2 The Neyman–Pearson test

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.2 — Neyman–Pearson lemma]{.tag} Let $p_0, p_1$ be the densities of $y$ under the two hypotheses. Consider the likelihood-ratio test (LRT) that decides $\mathcal H_1$ when
$$
p_1(y) > \eta\, p_0(y),
$$
with $\eta$ chosen so that its false-alarm probability equals $\alpha$. Among all tests with $P_{FA} \leq \alpha$, the LRT has the largest $P_D$.

::: proof
Let $\phi^\star$ be the indicator of the LRT and $\phi$ any test with $P_{FA}(\phi) \leq \alpha$. The integrand below is non-negative everywhere, because $\phi^\star = 1$ exactly where $p_1 - \eta p_0 > 0$:
$$
\int (\phi^\star - \phi)(p_1 - \eta\, p_0)\, dy \geq 0 .
$$

Expanding the integral gives
$$
P_D(\phi^\star) - P_D(\phi) \geq \eta\, \big(\alpha - P_{FA}(\phi)\big) \geq 0,
$$
which is the claim. [∎]{.qed}
:::

Two consequences shape the chapter. For a *known* signal, the log-ratio is linear in $\mathrm{Re}\langle y, s \rangle$: the LRT is the matched filter of Theorem 1.9. For an *unknown* Gaussian signal, $s[n] \sim \mathcal{CN}(0, P_s)$, both densities depend on $y$ only through $\|y\|^2$, and the ratio increases with it: the LRT is the **energy detector**.
::::

### 5.3 The energy detector and its SNR wall

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.3 — Energy detector]{.tag} Let $T = \sum_{n=1}^N |y[n]|^2$, with a Gaussian signal, a known noise power and many samples. By the central limit theorem, $T$ is nearly Gaussian, with mean $N\sigma^2$ and standard deviation $\sqrt N \sigma^2$ under $\mathcal H_0$.

Under $\mathcal H_1$ both are multiplied by $1 + \gamma$.

With $Q$ the Gaussian tail function, the threshold and the detection probability are
$$
\lambda = \sigma^2 \big(N + \sqrt N\, Q^{-1}(P_{FA})\big), \qquad P_D = Q\Big(\frac{Q^{-1}(P_{FA}) - \sqrt N\, \gamma}{1 + \gamma}\Big).
$$
Reaching a target $P_D$ requires a number of samples that grows like $1/\gamma^2$:
$$
N = \Big(\frac{Q^{-1}(P_{FA}) - (1 + \gamma)\, Q^{-1}(P_D)}{\gamma}\Big)^2 .
$$

::: proof
Proposition 0.4 gives the exact law $2T/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{2N}$ under $\mathcal H_0$, with the moments above. Under $\mathcal H_1$ the samples are $\mathcal{CN}(0, \sigma^2(1 + \gamma))$, so the same law holds with the power $\sigma^2 (1 + \gamma)$.

Normalising $T$, solving $P(T > \lambda) = P_{FA}$ under $\mathcal H_0$, then computing $P(T > \lambda)$ under $\mathcal H_1$ gives the formulas. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 5.4 — Sensing budget]{.tag} Target $P_{FA} = 0.01$ and $P_D = 0.9$, so that $Q^{-1}(P_{FA}) = 2.326$ and $Q^{-1}(P_D) = -1.282$.

-   At $\gamma = -10$ dB, that is $0.1$:
$$
N = \Big(\frac{2.326 + 1.1 \times 1.282}{0.1}\Big)^2 \approx 1\,396 \text{ samples}.
$$
-   At $-20$ dB the requirement is about $100$ times larger, about $1.3 \times 10^5$ samples.

Code 5.8 checks the first case by Monte Carlo.
:::

The formula promises detection at any SNR if one waits long enough. Real receivers only know the noise power approximately, and this breaks the promise.

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.5 — SNR wall (Tandra and Sahai, 2008)]{.tag} Suppose the noise power is only known to lie in $[\sigma_n^2 / \rho,\ \rho\, \sigma_n^2]$ for some $\rho > 1$. Then no energy detector achieves given $P_{FA} < 1/2 < P_D$ for all noise levels, however large $N$, when
$$
\gamma < \frac{\rho^2 - 1}{\rho}.
$$

::: proof
As $N \to \infty$, the average $T/N$ tends to the received power (law of large numbers).

1.  To keep $P_{FA}$ below $1/2$ at the worst noise level $\rho \sigma_n^2$, the threshold on $T/N$ must eventually exceed $\rho \sigma_n^2$.
2.  Under $\mathcal H_1$ with the most favourable noise level, $T/N$ tends to the limit
$$
\frac{\sigma_n^2}{\rho} + \gamma\, \sigma_n^2 .
$$
3.  Detection with $P_D > 1/2$ requires this limit to exceed the threshold, that is $\gamma > \rho - 1/\rho$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

A noise uncertainty of only 1 dB gives $\rho = 1.259$ and a wall at $\gamma = 0.465$, that is $-3.3$ dB.
::::

### 5.4 Feature detectors: exploiting the structure of the signal

Man-made signals are not Gaussian noise: they have carriers, symbol rates, pilots and cyclic prefixes. **Cyclostationary** detectors (Gardner, 1991) use the periodicity of their correlation.

::: def
[Definition 5.6 — Cyclic autocorrelation]{.tag} For a cyclic frequency $\alpha$ and a lag $\ell$,
$$
R_y^\alpha(\ell) = \lim_{N \to \infty} \frac1N \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} y[n + \ell]\, \overline{y[n]}\, e^{-2i\pi \alpha n}.
$$
Stationary noise has $R_w^\alpha = 0$ for every $\alpha \neq 0$, whereas a linearly modulated signal has non-zero values at multiples of its symbol rate. A test on $R_y^\alpha$ at those $\alpha$ is therefore insensitive to the noise level, and escapes the wall of Proposition 5.5.
:::

The price is knowledge: the detector must know which $\alpha$ to look at. Eigenvalue-based detectors (Zeng and Liang, 2009) use instead the structure of the sample covariance matrix.

### 5.5 Learned detectors

A learned detector is a classifier trained on labelled windows from $\mathcal H_0$ and $\mathcal H_1$ — raw IQ samples, spectra or spectrograms. O'Shea, Corgan and Clancy (2016) showed that a CNN on raw IQ samples recognises modulations from synthetic data as well as or better than expert features; O'Shea, Roy and Clancy (2018) extended this to over-the-air recordings.

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.7 — A calibrated classifier is a likelihood-ratio test]{.tag} If a classifier outputs the posterior probability $q(y) = P(\mathcal H_1 \mid y)$ and the classes have priors $\pi_0, \pi_1$, then
$$
\frac{q(y)}{1 - q(y)} = \frac{\pi_1}{\pi_0}\, \frac{p_1(y)}{p_0(y)} .
$$
Thresholding $q$ is a likelihood-ratio test; the Neyman–Pearson threshold is set on noise-only validation data for the target $P_{FA}$.

::: proof
Bayes' formula gives $q = \pi_1 p_1 / (\pi_0 p_0 + \pi_1 p_1)$, and the odds are an increasing function of the likelihood ratio. [∎]{.qed}
:::

A network therefore cannot beat the LRT *on the model it was trained on*. It wins when no tractable model exists — unknown modulations, coloured or impulsive noise, hardware effects — and loses when the test distribution drifts away from training.
::::

```python
# Code 5.8 — energy detector: Monte Carlo against the Gaussian approximation
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import norm

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
N, pfa, snr_db = 1_000, 0.01, -10.0
g = 10 ** (snr_db / 10)                              # SNR as a ratio, 0.1
lam = N + np.sqrt(N) * norm.isf(pfa)                 # threshold (noise power 1)
pd_theory = norm.sf((norm.isf(pfa) - np.sqrt(N) * g) / (1 + g))

def cn(shape, power=1.0):                            # circular complex Gaussian samples
    return np.sqrt(power / 2) * (rng.normal(size=shape) + 1j * rng.normal(size=shape))

T0 = np.sum(np.abs(cn((5_000, N))) ** 2, axis=1)                      # H0: noise only
T1 = np.sum(np.abs(cn((5_000, N), g) + cn((5_000, N))) ** 2, axis=1)  # H1: Gaussian signal
print(f"threshold {lam:.1f}; P_FA {np.mean(T0 > lam):.3f} (target {pfa})")
print(f"P_D Monte Carlo {np.mean(T1 > lam):.3f}, Gaussian approximation {pd_theory:.3f}")
n_req = ((norm.isf(pfa) - (1 + g) * norm.isf(0.9)) / g) ** 2
print(f"samples needed for P_D = 0.9 at -10 dB: {n_req:.0f}")
```

The simulated false-alarm rate is 0.009 for a target of 0.01, and the detection rate is 0.787 against 0.776 predicted; 1 396 samples reach a detection rate of 0.9.

The second experiment takes a narrowband primary user: a tone of unknown frequency and phase at $-15$ dB, observed over 256 samples. It compares the energy detector, the maximum of the periodogram (the generalised likelihood-ratio test for an unknown frequency) and a logistic regression trained on the 32 largest periodogram values — a shift-invariant representation, like the global pooling of Proposition 4.5.

```python
# Code 5.9 — classical versus learned detection of a narrowband signal
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
N, snr_db, m = 256, -15.0, 4_000
a = np.sqrt(10 ** (snr_db / 10))                     # tone amplitude, noise power 1

def draw(m):
    y = rng.integers(0, 2, m)
    n = np.arange(N)
    f = rng.uniform(0, 1, (m, 1))                    # unknown normalised frequency
    tone = a * np.exp(2j * np.pi * (f * n + rng.uniform(0, 1, (m, 1))))
    w = (rng.normal(size=(m, N)) + 1j * rng.normal(size=(m, N))) / np.sqrt(2)
    return w + y[:, None] * tone, y

def periodogram(x):
    P = np.abs(np.fft.fft(x, 4 * N, axis=1)) ** 2 / N   # zero-padded periodogram
    return np.sort(P, axis=1)[:, ::-1][:, :32]          # 32 largest values: shift-invariant

xtr, ytr = draw(m)
xte, yte = draw(m)
energy = np.sum(np.abs(xte) ** 2, axis=1)               # energy detector
glrt = np.max(np.abs(np.fft.fft(xte, 4 * N, axis=1)) ** 2, axis=1)   # max periodogram
clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2_000).fit(np.log(periodogram(xtr)), ytr)
learned = clf.decision_function(np.log(periodogram(xte)))
for name, s in [("energy", energy), ("max-periodogram", glrt), ("learned", learned)]:
    print(f"{name:16s} AUC {roc_auc_score(yte, s):.3f}")
```

The energy detector reaches an AUC of $0.64$; the periodogram peak and the learned detector both reach $0.82$. Physics (a model of the tone) and learning (on a representation with the right invariance) find the same structure. Learning would keep its edge if the signal were a mixture of unknown modulations, where no closed-form test exists.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 5
:::

-   Spectrum sensing is a binary test at negative SNR; the Neyman–Pearson LRT is optimal for a given false-alarm rate.
-   Known signal: matched filter. Unknown Gaussian signal: energy detector, whose sample size grows like $1/\gamma^2$.
-   Noise-power uncertainty creates an SNR wall, $-3.3$ dB for 1 dB of uncertainty.
-   Feature detectors (cyclostationarity, covariance structure) exploit signal structure and escape the wall.
-   A calibrated classifier is a likelihood-ratio test on its training distribution; set its threshold on noise-only data.
::::

## 6. Use case: radar emitter identification {#ch6}

An electronic-support receiver listens to the radars around it: it intercepts a stream of pulses from several emitters, interleaved in time, and must say how many radars there are, of which types, and possibly which individual transmitters. This chapter models the pulses, separates the trains with clustering and timing histograms, and discusses what learning adds.

### 6.1 Operational context and physics of pulsed radars

A pulsed radar emits pulses of width $\tau$ every pulse repetition interval (PRI) $T_r$. The receiver measures each intercepted pulse and summarises it by a small vector.

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — Pulse descriptor word]{.tag} A pulse descriptor word (PDW) gathers the measured parameters of one pulse: time of arrival (TOA), carrier frequency (RF), pulse width (PW), amplitude, angle of arrival (AOA), and possibly a description of the modulation inside the pulse. An interception produces a sequence of PDWs sorted by TOA, mixing all the emitters in view.
:::

::: ex
[Example 6.2 — Orders of magnitude]{.tag}

-   A PRI of 1 ms gives an unambiguous range of $c T_r / 2 = 150$ km; a pulse of 1 µs gives a range resolution of $c\tau/2 = 150$ m without compression (ch. 1.6).
-   The radar sees its echo after a two-way path, with a power decaying like $R^{-4}$; the interceptor receives the direct pulse, decaying like $R^{-2}$ (Friis formula).
-   This advantage lets an interceptor detect a radar well beyond the range at which the radar detects it, which is why electronic support exists.
:::

Emitters are classified by their **PRI pattern** — constant, jittered, staggered (a repeated sequence of PRIs), sliding or dwell-and-switch — together with RF agility and intrapulse modulation (Wiley's book on ELINT describes them).

### 6.2 Deinterleaving by timing: TOA-difference histograms

When several radars share a frequency band and a direction, the PDW parameters do not separate them; their *timing* does.

::: def
[Definition 6.3 — Difference histogram]{.tag} For TOAs $t_1 < t_2 < \dots$, the difference histogram counts the differences $t_j - t_i$, $j > i$, falling in each bin of width $b$, up to a maximum lag. The difference histogram of *order* $c$ keeps only the differences $t_{i+c} - t_i$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.4 — Peaks reveal the PRIs]{.tag}

1.  A single train $t_n = \varphi + n T$, $n = 0, \dots, M - 1$, produces the differences $kT$ only, with multiplicity $M - k$.
2.  For two interleaved trains with PRIs $T_1, T_2$ of irrational ratio, every difference between a pulse of one train and a pulse of the other occurs at most once.

The histogram therefore shows peaks at the multiples of each PRI over a flat floor of cross-differences.

::: proof
1.  A difference of two pulses $n$ and $n + k$ equals $kT$, and $M - k$ pairs have index gap $k$.
